The story behind an idea

Victor of Aveyron, the wild boy

In 1800 a boy who could not speak emerged from a French forest. A young doctor spent five years educating him.

In January 1800, a boy of about twelve appeared in the French department of Aveyron, naked and without speech, apparently having lived alone in the forest. He was taken to Paris, where many considered him a hopeless case.

Itard's experiment

Jean Marc Gaspard Itard, a physician at the Institute for Deaf-Mutes, thought otherwise. For five years he worked with the boy, whom he named Victor, using exercises to awaken his senses, attention and language. Victor learned to recognise some written words and to communicate in limited ways, but he never learned to speak.

Whether Victor had a pre-existing disability or autism, or whether isolation at a critical stage prevented language, is still debated. Itard's methods inspired Édouard Séguin and Maria Montessori, and the story was filmed as The Wild Child (1970) by François Truffaut.

References

  1. Itard, J. M. G. (1801). De l'éducation d'un homme sauvage. Goujon.
  2. Lane, H. (1976). The Wild Boy of Aveyron. Harvard University Press.
